newsitem.title: USA: Lott tells Democrats stop pouting about inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Lott tells Democrats stop pouting about inquiry.

text.p: Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said Wednesday minority Democrats should stop pouting about a Republican-ordered investigation of last November's disputed Senate race in Louisiana.

Democrat Mary Landrieu was certified as the winner over Republican Louis "Woody" Jenkins by 5,788 votes in the Nov. 5 election and was sworn in Jan. 7. But Jenkins says her victory was due to widespread voter fraud and wants the Senate to overturn the result and order a new election.

The Republican majority on the Senate Rules Committee voted last week for a full-scale investigation of the election over strong Democratic protests that Jenkins had not produced evidence to back up his charges.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said Friday Democrats would filibuster any attempt by Republicans to unseat Landrieu. Republicans have a 55-45 majority but it takes 60 votes to end a filibuster.
"The minority in the Senate seems to be inclined these days to any time they don't get their way to stomp their feet, pout, threaten," Lott, of Mississippi, said at a news conference.

"I would suggest to the minority that they grow up a little bit, realise they're in the minority, they're not going to get their way every time, and they should not expect to make irrational and irresponsible comments and not have us respond or act on them," Lott said.

"For instance, when the minority leader says that there's no way, no situation in which the election in Louisiana would be found to, in effect, have been involved in a pattern of fraud and a new election ordered, that's irresponsible.

"The issue is not Senator Landrieu or Woody Jenkins, the issue is what happened in the election. Was there a pattern of fraud in the election? We should not prejudge the results. We should go down, take a look on the scene as to what happened and get that information and make a decision," he said.
Daschle, at a separate news conference, said when asked about Lott's comments, "That isn't worthy of a response."
Investigators hired by the Rules Committee are expected to leave soon for Louisiana to question voters and election officials.
